svg.title: Three ways to make a Nova instance network-boot, and the single OpenCHAMI chain they all feed
svg.desc: Nova only ever assigns a boot index to storage devices, so there is no way to put a NIC in a guest's boot order and no equivalent of libvirt's boot order of disk then network. Every option in this section is therefore a way of getting something other than the NIC to start the network boot. Three candidates are tested in order. Test 1, in section 7.2, gives a UEFI guest an empty disk and lets the firmware run out of boot options and enumerate the NIC itself; if it works, coresmd serves the iPXE binary over TFTP and no OpenStack is involved in the boot chain at all. Test 2, in section 7.2b, gives the instance two storage devices in a known order — a blank root disk at boot index 0 and the iPXE ISO as a CD-ROM volume at boot index 1 — so the empty disk fails and iPXE runs. Test 3, in section 7.5, puts the instance into Nova stable device rescue mode with an iPXE image, which adds the boot media while keeping the node's own disks in their original order. Whichever of the three works, everything after it is identical and is unmodified OpenCHAMI: iPXE starts, CoreDHCP answers with the address SMD holds for that MAC and points at BSS, iPXE fetches the boot script BSS holds for that MAC, downloads the Talos kernel and initramfs from the head node's S3 store and boots them into RAM, enters maintenance mode and fetches its machine config from the talos.config URL on the kernel command line, then selects its install disk by size rather than by device name and writes itself to it. Each mechanism then has its own way back to booting from disk in section 10: reboot after Test 1, nothing at all after Test 2, unrescue after Test 3, or repointing the BSS payload at an iPXE sanboot script in the section 7.7 fallback. On real hardware all of this is one Redfish call setting the boot source override target to PXE followed by a reset.
svg.text: §7 — three ways to press “PXE”, and the one chain all three feed
Amber is the part that exists only because this is a cloud. Blue is ordinary, unmodified OpenCHAMI — it is identical on the PTR, and identical whichever amber door you came through.
THE CONSTRAINT — WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS AT ALL
Nova only ever assigns a boot_index to storage. There is no way to tell it to put a NIC in a guest's boot order, and no
equivalent of the libvirt lab's --boot uefi,hd,network. So all three options below are ways of getting
something other than the NIC to start the network boot.
On real hardware this is one call, not a section
BootSourceOverrideTarget=Pxe, then Reset. Everything
in amber is the hand-cranked equivalent of those two
Redfish fields — and appendix A makes them real again.
THE OPENSTACK-SPECIFIC PART — THREE CANDIDATE MECHANISMS
Test in this order. The first one that works deletes the other two.
TEST 1 · §7.2 · ~5 MIN
The firmware tries the network
A UEFI guest with an empty disk runs out of boot
options and enumerates the NIC on its own.
hw_firmware_type=uefi + tw-blank
If it works: libvirt-lab parity, and take it.
coresmd serves the iPXE binary over TFTP itself, so
there is no OpenStack in the boot chain at all.
Deletes §7.3, §7.5, §7.6. Nothing else changes.
TEST 2 · §7.2b · ~30 MIN
iPXE as a second boot device
Nova cannot order NICs, but it can order two
storage devices: blank disk 0, iPXE CD-ROM 1.
device_type=cdrom,boot_index=1
If it works: no rescue semantics, ever.
The empty disk fails, iPXE runs, Talos installs — and
from the next boot the disk is bootable and wins.
Deletes §7.5, §7.6. Costs one Cinder volume per node.
TEST 3 · §7.5 · ~10 MIN
Nova stable device rescue
Adds the iPXE ISO as boot media and keeps the
node's own disks in their original order.
--os-compute-api-version 2.87 … rescue
The proven path here — and the fallback.
sushy-tools implements Redfish Pxe by doing exactly
this, so appendix A needs it to work regardless.
Most moving parts, and a §10 sequence to remember.
whichever one works, everything below is byte-for-byte the same
UNMODIFIED OPENCHAMI — NOTHING BELOW HERE IS CLOUD-SPECIFIC
iPXE is running
iPXE 1.x.x+ -- Open Source Network Boot Firmware -- https://ipxe.org
The one console line that proves the OpenStack half of the chain. Past it you
no longer care which of the three mechanisms produced it.
CoreDHCP answers — §5.7, from SMD's record — §6
The address SMD holds for 52:54:00:be:ef:01, and the lease also carries the
BSS URL. A 172.16.0.2xx address is a bootloop lease — the MAC is unknown.
iPXE chains to BSS — §9
http://172.16.0.254:8081/boot/v1/bootscript?mac=52:54:00:be:ef:01 … ok
The script is keyed on the MAC, so the node's role comes from its NIC — never
from the Nova instance name you typed. §6's offset-by-one table matters here.
Talos kernel and initramfs, from the head's S3 — §8
:7070/boot-images/talos/vmlinuz-amd64 · initramfs-amd64.xz … ok
Booted into RAM. There is no image to build and nothing on the node's disk yet,
which is exactly why an empty root disk is the right starting state.
Maintenance mode, then the machine config
talos.config=http://172.16.0.254:7070/…/controlplane.yaml
No cloud-init, no SSH key, no user-data. The config arrives on the kernel
command line, which is what keeps OpenCHAMI the source of truth, not Nova.
Talos writes itself to the node's own disk — §8.6
diskSelector: { size: '>= 10GB' } — by description, never /dev/vda
Under rescue the node has two disks, so a fixed device name is a guess. This is
why “disks keep their original order” is a requirement and not a nicety.
AND THE WAY BACK — “BOOT FROM DISK”, IN §10
Same three doors, in reverse. Record which one you used: §10, appendix A and the IaC all branch on it.
After Test 1 — firmware
openstack server reboot
The disk is bootable now, so the firmware
prefers it and never reaches the NIC.
After Test 2 — CD-ROM
(nothing)
The disk is boot_index=0 and wins from
the next boot. No state anywhere.
After Test 3 — rescue
openstack server unrescue
Always unrescue before stop — Nova
refuses to stop a rescued instance.
§7.7 fallback — iPXE always
sanboot --drive 0x80
BSS gains a third payload, and “is this
node installed?” becomes BSS's state.
The ordering constraint — the one way to waste an afternoon here
Do not press PXE before §8 and §9 exist. A node that network-boots with nothing in BSS gets its lease, asks what to do, is told nothing, and stops — which on the
console looks almost exactly like a broken DHCP chain. Publish the Talos assets and the boot payloads first; §7.5 is a dry run, and it is meant to fail at step 3.
The whole deviation is at most two commands wide — everything in blue is what will happen unchanged on the PTR, where a BMC replaces both amber bands.
